questions.stem: A 61 year old man has had a slow recovery after a hip replacement and is anxious about going home. His GP spends extra time arranging home physiotherapy, adjusts his analgesia so he can mobilise, and refers him for a falls assessment, explaining that each step should help him get back to walking his dog. He agrees to the plan.
questions.q: Which ethical principle is the doctor mainly acting on?
o: Autonomy
Beneficence
Confidentiality
Justice
Non-maleficence
questions.e: Actively acting in the patient's best interests to improve his wellbeing is beneficence.

steps.x: The question asks: Which ethical principle is the doctor mainly acting on?
The doctor is actively promoting his good.

elim: He agrees, but the doctor's actions are driven by promoting his wellbeing.
No information is being shared or withheld.
This is not about fair allocation between patients.
The focus is actively doing good, not avoiding a harm.

steps.x: B: Beneficence. Beneficence = doing good; non-maleficence = avoiding harm.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man who is homeless and has a history of alcohol use needs a hernia repair. A colleague suggests he should go to the back of the waiting list because he may not attend follow-up. The consultant insists he is listed in the same order and by the same clinical criteria as every other patient.
questions.q: Which ethical principle is the consultant mainly upholding?
o: Autonomy
Beneficence
Confidentiality
Justice
Non-maleficence
questions.e: Equal treatment and fair allocation of resources, regardless of background, is justice.

steps.x: The question asks: Which ethical principle is the consultant mainly upholding?

clues: same order and by the same clinical criteria as every other patient
steps.x: Equal treatment of all patients.

elim: The issue is not his right to choose.
The point is fairness between patients, not his benefit alone.
No disclosure is involved.
The point is equal treatment, not avoiding harm.

steps.x: D: Justice. Justice = fair allocation and equal treatment.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with frailty has advanced bowel cancer. Her oncologist explains that a further course of chemotherapy might extend her life by a few months, but would very likely cause severe nausea, infections and hospital admissions. The team discuss how to balance the possible gain against the likely harm before advising her.
questions.q: Which two ethical principles are most in tension?
o: Autonomy and justice
Beneficence and justice
Beneficence and non-maleficence
Confidentiality and autonomy
Justice and non-maleficence
questions.e: Possible benefit (beneficence) is weighed against likely harm (non-maleficence); ethics balances pillars sensibly.

steps.x: The question asks: Which two ethical principles are most in tension?

clues: very likely cause severe nausea, infections
steps.x: Gain versus harm.

elim: Neither her choice nor resources is the issue described.
Resource allocation is not discussed.
No information sharing is involved.
Fair allocation is not the issue.

steps.x: C: Beneficence and non-maleficence. Benefit vs harm = beneficence vs non-maleficence; balance them for the situation.

questions.stem: A 81 year old man with acute delirium from a urinary infection needs a urinary catheter. When the procedure, its purpose and its risks are explained in simple words with a diagram, he says he is at a train station and cannot follow what is being said. He repeats clearly that he does not want 'anything'.
questions.q: Which element of the capacity assessment is he unable to meet?
o: Communicate a decision
None, he has capacity
Retain the information
Understand the information
Weigh up the information
questions.e: He cannot understand the relevant information despite simple explanation, so he lacks capacity for this decision.

steps.x: The question asks: Which element of the capacity assessment is he unable to meet?

clues: cannot follow what is being said
steps.x: No understanding, but clear communication.

elim: He clearly communicates 'no'.
He cannot get as far as retaining it; he does not take it in.
He cannot weigh what he has not understood.
All four elements must be met; he fails the first.

steps.x: D: Understand the information. Understand, retain, weigh, communicate: failing any one means no capacity.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a large brainstem stroke. She is awake and appears to follow conversation but cannot speak, write, blink to command or use any communication aid despite help from speech and language therapists. A decision is needed about inserting a feeding tube.
questions.q: Which element of the capacity assessment is she unable to meet?
o: Communicate the decision
None, she has capacity
Retain the information
Understand the information
Weigh up the information
questions.e: Capacity needs the decision to be communicated by any means; with no means despite support, she fails this element.

steps.x: The question asks: Which element of the capacity assessment is she unable to meet?

clues: cannot speak, write, blink to command or use any communication aid
steps.x: Every route of communication has been tried.

elim: There is no evidence she cannot retain it.
She appears to follow conversation.
Cannot be shown either way, but the clear failure is communication.
All four elements must be met; she cannot communicate any decision.

steps.x: A: Communicate the decision. Communication by any means counts; with none at all, capacity is absent.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has delirium due to pneumonia that fluctuates through the day. In the morning he cannot understand the information about a planned elective hernia repair. By the afternoon he is alert and orientated. The operation is not urgent.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate statement about his capacity?
o: He has capacity for all decisions because he is alert at times
He lacks capacity because he has delirium
He permanently lacks capacity for this decision
His family can consent for him
It should be reassessed when he is more alert
questions.e: Capacity is time-specific: with a non-urgent decision, reassess when he is at his best.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most accurate statement about his capacity?
Fluctuating capacity and no urgency.

elim: Capacity is decision- and time-specific.
A diagnosis alone does not remove capacity.
Delirium is temporary and fluctuating.
Relatives cannot consent for an adult.

steps.x: E: It should be reassessed when he is more alert. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder refuses a blood transfusion for an Hb of 52 g/L because she believes donated blood is 'contaminated'. She can explain the risks of refusing, repeat them an hour later and states her decision clearly. She cannot use the information because the contamination fear overrides everything.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate conclusion about her capacity for this decision?
o: She has capacity because she can communicate clearly
She has capacity because she meets three of the four elements
She lacks capacity because she has a mental illness
She lacks capacity for all decisions
She lacks capacity for this decision
questions.e: She understands, retains and communicates but cannot weigh up; all four are needed, so she lacks capacity for this decision.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most accurate conclusion about her capacity for this decision?
Three elements met, weighing failed.

elim: All four elements must be met.
Communication is only one element.
Capacity is decision-specific.
Diagnosis alone does not remove capacity; it is the failure to weigh.

steps.x: E: She lacks capacity for this decision. All four elements (understand, retain, weigh, communicate) must be satisfied.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man tells his psychiatrist in clinic that he has bought a knife and plans to kill his former partner tonight because she has a new boyfriend. He asks the psychiatrist to keep this between them. He has capacity and is not psychotic.
questions.q: Which is the main justification for breaching his confidentiality?
o: Court order
Notifiable disease
Patient consent
Public interest in research
Risk of serious harm to others
questions.e: Confidentiality can be breached when there is a risk of serious harm to others.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main justification for breaching his confidentiality?

clues: plans to kill his former partner tonight
steps.x: A specific threat of serious violence.

elim: No court has ordered disclosure.
No infectious disease is involved.
He has refused consent.
Not a reason to breach confidentiality here.

steps.x: E: Risk of serious harm to others. Serious risk of harm to the patient or others justifies disclosure.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman is the defendant in a criminal trial. The judge issues a court order for her GP to provide copies of her medical records relevant to the case. The woman tells the GP she does not want the records shared. The GP checks the order is valid and limits what is released to what the order requires.
questions.q: Which is the main justification for disclosing the records?
o: Legal requirement to disclose
Patient consent
Risk of serious harm to others
Risk of serious harm to the patient
Safeguarding concern
questions.e: A court order is a legal requirement to disclose, one of the exceptions to confidentiality.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main justification for disclosing the records?
The law requires it.

elim: She has refused.
No threat of harm is described.
No risk to her is described.
No vulnerable person is at risk.

steps.x: A: Legal requirement to disclose. Legal requirements (court order, notifiable disease) override confidentiality.

questions.stem: A 19 year old student starts a consultation with a new GP by asking her to promise that nothing he says will ever be passed on to anyone, under any circumstances. He wants to discuss his mental health. The GP wants to give him an honest answer before he continues.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate statement about confidentiality?
o: It applies only to adults over 21
It can be breached whenever a relative asks
It is a core duty but not absolute
It is absolute and can never be broken
It is waived for mental health problems
questions.e: Confidentiality is a core duty but not absolute: risk of serious harm, safeguarding and legal duties are exceptions.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most accurate statement about confidentiality?

clues: promise that nothing he says will ever be passed on
steps.x: He wants an absolute promise.

elim: It applies to all patients, including young people.
Relatives have no automatic right to information.
There are recognised exceptions.
Mental health information is confidential too.

steps.x: C: It is a core duty but not absolute. Confidentiality is not absolute; never promise total secrecy.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man with long-standing schizophrenia, stable on clozapine, is advised to have an inguinal hernia repair. He declines, saying he would rather wait and see because he is worried about time off work. The surgical registrar suggests that his schizophrenia means he cannot make the decision.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Ask his mother to consent for him
Assess his capacity for this decision using the four-stage test
Detain him under the Mental Health Act
Proceed with surgery in his best interests
Record that he lacks capacity because of his diagnosis
questions.e: Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed (understand, retain, weigh, communicate), not assumed from a diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step?

clues: his schizophrenia means he cannot make the decision
steps.x: A diagnosis is being used to assume incapacity.

elim: Relatives cannot consent for an adult.
That is for treating mental disorder, not a hernia.
Best interests only applies if he lacks capacity.
A diagnosis alone does not mean lack of capacity.

steps.x: B: Assess his capacity for this decision using the four-stage test. Assess capacity for the specific decision; never assume from a diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman with mild dementia is being assessed for capacity to consent to cataract surgery. She has just listened to an explanation of the operation and its risks and can describe it accurately. The doctor now wants to test the next element of the four-stage test.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to test this?
o: Ask her how she balanced the risks and benefits
Ask her to describe the risks again later in the conversation
Ask her to indicate her decision
Ask her to name the Prime Minister
Perform an abbreviated mental test
questions.e: After understanding comes retaining: can she hold the information long enough to make the decision?

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to test this?
Understanding is shown; next is retaining.

elim: That tests weighing, the third element.
That tests communication, the fourth element.
Orientation is not an element of the capacity test.
A cognitive score does not test decision-specific capacity.

steps.x: B: Ask her to describe the risks again later in the conversation. Order: understand, retain, weigh, communicate.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man needs to decide whether to have a below-knee amputation for an infected, ischaemic foot. He can explain the operation and its risks and repeat them later. The doctor now wants to know whether he can use this information to reach a decision.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate question to ask him?
o: Can you repeat what I just told you?
Do you know what day it is?
How have you balanced the risks of the operation against the risks of not having it?
What would your family want you to do?
Will you sign the consent form?
questions.e: Weighing up means using the information to balance options and reach a decision.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate question to ask him?

clues: use this information to reach a decision
steps.x: This is the weighing element.

elim: Tests understanding or retention, already shown.
Orientation is not part of the capacity test.
Does not test his own weighing of the decision.
Tests communicating a decision, not weighing.

steps.x: C: How have you balanced the risks of the operation against the risks of not having it?. Weigh up = balancing risks and benefits to reach a decision.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with a moderate learning disability is offered a dental extraction under local anaesthetic. His carer is present. The dentist explains the procedure using pictures and simple language and wants to begin the first element of the capacity assessment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to begin?
o: Ask him to explain in his own words what will happen
Ask him to repeat the risks 30 minutes later
Ask him to sign the consent form
Ask his carer whether he understands
Ask what he thinks his carer would choose
questions.e: The first element is understanding the relevant information, tested by asking him to explain it back.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to begin?
Start with understanding.

elim: The patient must be assessed directly.
Tests retention, the second element.
Tests communication, not understanding.
Does not test understanding.

steps.x: A: Ask him to explain in his own words what will happen. Understanding is tested by explaining it back in his own words.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman is unconscious on intensive care after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. A decision is needed about a tracheostomy. She has no advance decision and no lasting power of attorney. Her closest friend of 30 years visits daily; her brother, whom she has not spoken to for 20 years, phones as next of kin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to make the decision?
o: Ask her brother to sign a consent form as next of kin
Decide in her best interests after consulting her friend about her wishes
Let the consultant decide without consulting anyone
Postpone the decision until she regains capacity
Refer every decision to the Court of Protection
questions.e: For a patient lacking capacity, decide in her best interests, considering her past wishes and the views of those who know her well.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to make the decision?
No advance decision; one person knows her well.

elim: Next of kin cannot consent for an adult.
Those who know her well must be consulted.
The decision cannot safely wait.
Not needed routinely; best interests applies.

steps.x: B: Decide in her best interests after consulting her friend about her wishes. Best interests: past wishes and values, input from those who know her best.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman with advanced Alzheimer's disease lacks capacity to decide about surgery for a fractured neck of femur. Her daughter arrives with the consent form and says she will sign it on her mother's behalf. There is no lasting power of attorney for health.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask the daughter to sign the consent form
Delay surgery until her mother regains capacity
Make a best interests decision, involving her daughter
Proceed without telling the daughter
Treat her under the Mental Health Act
questions.e: Under the Mental Capacity Act, a best interests decision is made by the clinician, with input from family.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?

clues: she will sign it on her mother's behalf
steps.x: No legal proxy.

elim: Relatives cannot consent for an adult without a health LPA.
Advanced dementia will not improve; delay causes harm.
Those who know her should be consulted.
That is for mental disorder, not hip surgery.

steps.x: C: Make a best interests decision, involving her daughter. Family give views; the clinician decides in best interests under the MCA.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman with mild dementia attends with her son, who is her paid carer. She has unexplained bruises on both upper arms in different stages of healing and seems frightened when he speaks. While he is out of the room she says he 'gets rough' but asks the doctor not to say anything.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask her son to explain the bruises
Do nothing because she asked for confidentiality
Prescribe arnica cream and review in 2 weeks
Refer to the adult safeguarding team
Tell her son that the doctor suspects abuse
questions.e: Safeguarding concerns are a recognised reason to share information without consent.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?

clues: bruises on both upper arms in different stages of healing
steps.x: Likely elder abuse.

elim: May increase risk to her.
Safeguarding concerns justify sharing.
Ignores likely abuse.
May put her at greater risk.

steps.x: D: Refer to the adult safeguarding team. Safeguarding concerns justify breaching confidentiality.

questions.stem: A 7 year old unvaccinated boy has fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash spreading from behind the ears. His GP makes a clinical diagnosis of measles. His father asks that nobody outside the practice is told because the family are anti-vaccination.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask the father for written consent before notifying
Inform the boy's school directly
Keep the diagnosis confidential as requested
Notify only if the diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory testing
Notify the UK Health Security Agency
questions.e: Measles is a notifiable disease, so disclosure is a legal requirement without consent.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?

clues: nobody outside the practice is told
steps.x: A notifiable disease.

elim: Notification is a legal duty and does not need consent.
Public health, not the GP, manages contacts.
Measles is notifiable by law.
Notify on clinical suspicion.

steps.x: E: Notify the UK Health Security Agency. Notifiable diseases are a legal exception to confidentiality.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He refuses to tell his long-term female partner or use condoms, and says he will not change. The doctor has explained the risk to her and given him time and support, but he still refuses. His partner is not a patient at the practice.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Inform the partner, telling him first that this will happen
Inform the police
Keep his confidence because she is not a patient here
Notify his employer
Tell her without telling him
questions.e: A serious, identifiable risk of harm to another person can justify disclosure after attempts to persuade him have failed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?

clues: refuses to tell his long-term female partner
steps.x: Persistent risk of serious harm to a known person.

elim: Not the appropriate step for this risk.
A serious risk of harm to others can justify disclosure.
No reason to involve the employer.
He should be told first that disclosure will happen.

steps.x: A: Inform the partner, telling him first that this will happen. Serious harm to others justifies limited disclosure; tell the patient first.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with capacity is advised to have a coronary artery bypass graft for triple vessel disease. He understands, retains and weighs up the information, including the risk of death without surgery, and clearly says he does not want the operation. His wife pleads with the team to persuade him.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask his wife to consent on his behalf
Perform surgery in his best interests
Refer for a Mental Health Act assessment
Repeat the capacity assessment until he agrees
Respect his decision and document the discussion
questions.e: An adult with capacity can refuse treatment; respecting this upholds autonomy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?

clues: clearly says he does not want the operation
steps.x: A capacitous refusal.

elim: Relatives cannot consent for an adult with capacity.
Best interests applies only when capacity is lacking.
There is no mental disorder.
Capacity is not judged by agreeing with doctors.

steps.x: E: Respect his decision and document the discussion. A capacitous refusal must be respected (autonomy), even if unwise.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has been signed off work with depression. Her line manager phones the GP surgery, says he is worried about her, and asks what her diagnosis is and when she will be fit to return. The woman has not given consent for any information to be shared with her employer.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Confirm the diagnosis but not the treatment
Decline to share any information without her consent
Give the information because he is concerned
Share the expected return date only
Tell him she is a patient but nothing else
questions.e: With no risk of serious harm, safeguarding concern or legal requirement, information stays confidential.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate response?
No exception applies.

elim: Even confirming the diagnosis breaches confidentiality.
Concern alone is not an exception.
Still confidential information.
Even confirming she is a patient is a breach.

steps.x: B: Decline to share any information without her consent. Outside the exceptions, patient information stays confidential.

questions.stem: A medical student is preparing for a ward round. She is asked which piece of UK legislation sets out the four-stage test of capacity (understand, retain, weigh up, communicate) and the requirement that decisions for adults who lack capacity are made in their best interests.
questions.q: Which is the legal framework?
o: Children Act 1989
Equality Act 2010
Human Tissue Act 2004
Mental Capacity Act 2005
Mental Health Act 1983
questions.e: The Mental Capacity Act sets out the capacity test and best interests decisions in England and Wales.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the legal framework?
Capacity and best interests.

elim: Concerns the welfare of children.
Concerns discrimination.
Concerns tissue and organ removal and storage.
Concerns detention and treatment for mental disorder.

steps.x: D: Mental Capacity Act 2005. Capacity and best interests = Mental Capacity Act; detention for mental disorder = Mental Health Act.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman is offered a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Her surgeon explains the benefits, the risk of bile duct injury, and the option of not having surgery, and checks she has understood before she decides. The surgeon says this is so she can choose for herself.
questions.q: Which ethical principle is the main basis of informed consent?
o: Autonomy
Beneficence
Justice
Non-maleficence
Paternalism
questions.e: Informed consent respects the patient's right to make her own decisions: autonomy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which ethical principle is the main basis of informed consent?

clues: so she can choose for herself
steps.x: The point is her choice.

elim: Consent is about her right to choose, not the doctor acting for her good.
Fair allocation is not involved.
Explaining risks is not mainly about avoiding harm.
The opposite: the doctor deciding for the patient.

steps.x: A: Autonomy. Informed consent rests on autonomy.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man lacks capacity after a severe head injury. A best interests decision is needed about whether to continue long-term ventilation. His wife says he was a devout Catholic and often said he would 'never want to be kept alive on machines'. The team is listing the factors they must take into account.
questions.q: Which factor must be considered in his best interests decision?
o: His previously expressed wishes and beliefs
His wife's own preferences for her future
The consultant's own religious views
The cost of the intensive care bed
Whether he would be easy to look after
questions.e: Best interests must consider the patient's past wishes, values and beliefs, and the views of those who know him.

steps.x: The question asks: Which factor must be considered in his best interests decision?

clues: never want to be kept alive on machines
steps.x: His own past wishes and faith.

elim: The decision is about his interests, not hers.
The clinician's beliefs are not relevant.
Not a best interests factor for the individual.
Convenience is not part of best interests.

steps.x: A: His previously expressed wishes and beliefs. Best interests includes past wishes, values and beliefs.

questions.stem: A clinical commissioning panel has a fixed annual budget. It must decide whether to fund a very expensive new drug that gives one patient a small benefit, or use the same money to fund hip replacements for 40 patients on the waiting list. The panel weighs the benefit to each group fairly.
questions.q: Which ethical principle is most central to the panel's decision?
o: Autonomy
Beneficence
Confidentiality
Justice
Non-maleficence
questions.e: Fair allocation of limited resources is justice; it often has to be balanced against beneficence to individuals.

steps.x: The question asks: Which ethical principle is most central to the panel's decision?

clues: weighs the benefit to each group fairly
steps.x: Limited resources shared fairly.

elim: No individual patient's choice is the issue.
Benefit matters, but the core issue is fair distribution between patients.
No information is being shared.
Avoiding harm is not the main issue.

steps.x: D: Justice. Justice = fair allocation of resources.
